## Abstract

We study finite sets with a fixed-point-free involution, equipped with the octahedral simplicial structure in which faces are precisely the finite subsets containing no complete antipodal pair. An equivariant simplicial map is a vertex map commuting with the involutions and preserving this constraint. The coindex of such an object is the largest dimension of an octahedral sphere admitting an equivariant simplicial map into it. We prove that every equivariant simplicial map is vertex-injective. This gives a uniform cardinality obstruction: a map from the $m$-dimensional octahedral sphere into $K$ requires at least $2(m+1)$ vertices. We then classify every finite nonempty object as an octahedral sphere: if $K$ has $r$ antipodal orbits, then $K$ is equivariantly isomorphic to the boundary of the $r$-dimensional cross-polytope. Consequently,

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K)=r-1=\frac{|V(K)|}{2}-1.
$$

The coindex is therefore a complete invariant up to equivariant simplicial isomorphism in this model. We construct the join bifunctor, identify the join of two octahedral spheres with a sphere of dimension one greater than the sum of dimensions, and establish the sharp formula

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=\operatorname{coind}(K)+\operatorname{coind}(L)+1
$$

for all finite nonempty objects. We also prove monotonicity under equivariant simplicial maps, attainment of the defining maximum, commutativity and associativity at coindex level, and functoriality of join. Algorithms for classification, coindex computation, join formation, and map validation are provided, together with applications to non-compression, signed encodings, and coloring-type questions.

## 1. Introduction

Antipodal symmetry is one of the simplest nontrivial group actions. A free action of $\mathbb Z_2$ partitions a set into pairs, and this pairing supports combinatorial analogues of centrally symmetric spheres. Despite the elementary data, invariants defined through equivariant maps can resemble classical topological indices and may appear to demand global obstruction theory.

The present setting is deliberately specific. Given a free $\mathbb Z_2$-set, we declare a vertex subset to be a face exactly when it avoids containing both members of any antipodal pair. This is the octahedral, or cross-polytope-boundary, structure. Its specificity creates strong rigidity: equivariance and simpliciality together force every admissible map to be injective. The resulting theory is governed entirely by the number of antipodal orbits.

Our main structural result classifies every finite nonempty object in this model. If it has $r$ orbits, it is equivariantly simplicially isomorphic to the standard octahedral sphere of dimension $r-1$. Thus the coindex, initially defined as a supremum over source spheres, is simply $r-1$. This turns the join law into orbit arithmetic. The join has the disjoint union of the two vertex sets, hence the sum of their orbit counts, and the normalization from orbit count to dimension yields the correction term $+1$.

The restriction to the octahedral simplicial structure is essential. A general free simplicial $\mathbb Z_2$-complex may have many more restrictions on its faces, and its equivariant type need not be determined by the cardinality of its vertex orbits. Here, however, all allowable faces are generated by one rule—avoid antipodal pairs—and the classification is exact.

## 2. Definitions and basic constructions

### 2.1. Finite free $\mathbb Z_2$-sets

**Definition 2.1 (Free involutive vertex system).** A free $\mathbb Z_2$-set $K$ consists of a vertex set $V(K)$ and a map $\alpha_K:V(K)\to V(K)$ such that, for every $v\in V(K)$,

$$
\alpha_K(\alpha_K(v))=v
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\alpha_K(v)\ne v.
$$

We write $\bar v$ for $\alpha_K(v)$. The orbits are the pairs $\{v,\bar v\}$.

**Definition 2.2 (Octahedral simplicial structure).** The faces of $K$ are the finite subsets $\sigma\subseteq V(K)$ satisfying

$$
\text{there is no }v\text{ for which }\{v,\bar v\}\subseteq\sigma.
$$

Equivalently, a face contains at most one member of each antipodal orbit.

This convention makes every finite free involutive set into a simplicial complex without adding further data. If $K$ has $r$ orbits, its maximal faces have $r$ vertices.

### 2.2. Equivariant simplicial maps

**Definition 2.3 (Equivariant simplicial map).** A map $f:K\to L$ is a vertex function $f:V(K)\to V(L)$ satisfying:

1. **Equivariance:** $f(\bar v)=\overline{f(v)}$ for every $v$.
2. **Simpliciality:** whenever $f(p)=\overline{f(q)}$, one has $p=\bar q$.

The second condition is equivalent to preservation of all antipodal-pair-free faces. Indeed, a source face could fail to map to a target face only if two non-antipodal source vertices mapped to a complete antipodal pair.

Identity maps satisfy these conditions, and composites of such maps again satisfy them. An equivariant bijection is automatically an equivariant simplicial isomorphism, since injectivity converts antipodality of images into antipodality of sources.

### 2.3. Standard octahedral spheres

**Definition 2.4 (Octahedral sphere).** For $n\ge 0$, define

$$
S^n_{\mathrm{oct}}=\{(i,\varepsilon):0\le i\le n,\ \varepsilon\in\{+,-\}\},
$$

with antipode $\overline{(i,+)}=(i,-)$ and $\overline{(i,-)}=(i,+)$. Its simplicial structure forbids choosing both signs at a fixed coordinate.

This is the boundary complex of the $(n+1)$-dimensional cross-polytope, with signed unit vectors $\pm e_0,\ldots,\pm e_n$ as vertices.

**Lemma 2.5 (Cardinality of the standard sphere).** The octahedral sphere $S^n_{\mathrm{oct}}$ has

$$
|V(S^n_{\mathrm{oct}})|=2(n+1)
$$

vertices and $n+1$ antipodal orbits.

**Proof sketch.** There are $n+1$ coordinate labels and two signs for each label.

### 2.4. Coindex

**Definition 2.6 (Coindex).** For a free $\mathbb Z_2$-set $K$, define

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K)=
\sup\{m\in\mathbb N: S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\text{ admits an equivariant simplicial map into }K\}.
$$

For finite nonempty $K$, we shall prove that this supremum is finite, attained, and equal to the number of antipodal orbits minus one.

**Proposition 2.7 (Maps between standard spheres).** There exists an equivariant simplicial map

$$
S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\longrightarrow S^n_{\mathrm{oct}}
$$

if and only if $m\le n$. Consequently,

$$
\operatorname{coind}(S^n_{\mathrm{oct}})=n.
$$

**Proof sketch.** If $m\le n$, include the first $m+1$ signed coordinate pairs among the $n+1$ pairs. Conversely, the injectivity theorem below forces $2(m+1)\le2(n+1)$, hence $m\le n$.

## 3. Rigidity and the cardinality obstruction

### 3.1. Vertex injectivity

**Theorem 3.1 (Injectivity of equivariant simplicial maps).** Every equivariant simplicial map $f:K\to L$ is injective on vertices.

**Proof.** Suppose $f(p)=f(q)$. Equivariance and involutivity give

$$
f(q)=\overline{f(\bar q)}.
$$

Thus $f(p)=\overline{f(\bar q)}$. By simpliciality, $p=\overline{\bar q}=q$. Therefore $f$ is injective.

This short argument is the central rigidity principle. Equivariance alone permits an entire orbit to map to another orbit, while simpliciality alone need not prevent ordinary collisions. Together they prohibit every collision.

### 3.2. A finite Borsuk–Ulam-type bound

**Theorem 3.2 (Uniform vertex bound).** Let $K$ be finite. If there is an equivariant simplicial map $S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K$, then

$$
2(m+1)\le |V(K)|.
$$

**Proof.** By Theorem 3.1, the map is injective. Lemma 2.5 gives $2(m+1)$ source vertices, all of which must have distinct images in $K$.

The terminology “Borsuk–Ulam-type” refers to the role of equivariance as an obstruction to mapping a larger antipodal sphere into a smaller target. In this combinatorial model, the obstruction is stronger and more elementary than a topological coincidence theorem: admissible maps are outright injections.

**Corollary 3.3 (Boundedness).** For finite $K$, the set of integers $m$ admitting a map $S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K$ is bounded above.

**Proof sketch.** Theorem 3.2 implies $m+1\le |V(K)|/2$, and even the weaker bound $m\le |V(K)|$ suffices.

### 3.3. Attainment

**Lemma 3.4 (The zero-sphere maps into every nonempty object).** If $K$ contains a vertex $v$, then there is an equivariant simplicial map $S^0_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K$ sending the two source vertices to $v$ and $\bar v$.

**Proof sketch.** The assignment is equivariant by construction. The only antipodal image pair comes from the antipodal source pair, so it is simplicial.

**Theorem 3.5 (Attainment of coindex).** If $K$ is finite and nonempty, then an equivariant simplicial map

$$
S^{\operatorname{coind}(K)}_{\mathrm{oct}}\longrightarrow K
$$

exists.

**Proof sketch.** Lemma 3.4 makes the set in Definition 2.6 nonempty. Corollary 3.3 makes it a finite nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$, so its supremum is its maximum.

## 4. Classification and completeness of coindex

### 4.1. Orbit normal form

**Theorem 4.1 (Classification of finite nonempty objects).** Let $K$ be a finite nonempty free $\mathbb Z_2$-set with $r$ antipodal orbits. Then $r\ge1$, and there exists an equivariant simplicial isomorphism

$$
K\cong S^{r-1}_{\mathrm{oct}}.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Choose one representative $x_i$ from each antipodal orbit and enumerate them by $i=0,\ldots,r-1$. Every vertex is uniquely either $x_i$ or $\bar x_i$. Define

$$
x_i\longmapsto(i,+),
\qquad
\bar x_i\longmapsto(i,-).
$$

This is a bijection and commutes with antipodes. Because both source and target declare exactly the antipodal-pair-free subsets to be faces, the bijection and its inverse preserve faces. Hence it is an equivariant simplicial isomorphism.

The choice of representatives is not canonical, but existence is enough for classification. Different choices change signs or permute coordinate axes, operations that are themselves automorphisms of the standard sphere.

**Corollary 4.2 (Coindex formula).** If $K$ is finite and nonempty with $r$ antipodal orbits, then

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K)=r-1.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
2\bigl(\operatorname{coind}(K)+1\bigr)=|V(K)|.
$$

**Proof.** By Theorem 4.1, $K$ is isomorphic to $S^{r-1}_{\mathrm{oct}}$. Coindex is unchanged by equivariant simplicial isomorphism, and Proposition 2.7 gives coindex $r-1$. Since every orbit has two vertices, $|V(K)|=2r$.

**Corollary 4.3 (Completeness).** Two finite nonempty objects $K$ and $L$ are equivariantly simplicially isomorphic if and only if

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K)=\operatorname{coind}(L).
$$

**Proof sketch.** An isomorphism preserves coindex. Conversely, equal coindices imply equal orbit counts by Corollary 4.2, and Theorem 4.1 identifies both objects with the same standard octahedral sphere.

Thus coindex is not merely an obstruction or a lower-dimensional shadow. Within this category it is a complete invariant.

### 4.2. Monotonicity

**Theorem 4.4 (Monotonicity).** If $L$ is finite and there is an equivariant simplicial map $K\to L$, then

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K)\le\operatorname{coind}(L).
$$

**Proof sketch.** Any map $S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K$ composes with $K\to L$ to give a map $S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\to L$. Therefore every admissible dimension for $K$ is admissible for $L$, and the supremum cannot decrease. When both objects are finite and nonempty, Theorem 3.1 gives the equivalent cardinality argument $|V(K)|\le|V(L)|$.

## 5. Join and its exact coindex law

### 5.1. Join of objects and maps

**Definition 5.1 (Join).** The join $K*L$ has vertex set the disjoint union

$$
V(K*L)=V(K)\sqcup V(L),
$$

with the antipodal action inherited separately on each summand. Its faces are all antipodal-pair-free subsets of this disjoint union.

If $K$ and $L$ have $r$ and $s$ antipodal orbits, respectively, then $K*L$ has $r+s$ orbits.

**Definition 5.2 (Join of maps).** Given equivariant simplicial maps $f:A\to K$ and $g:B\to L$, define

$$
f*g:A*B\longrightarrow K*L
$$

by using $f$ on the $A$ summand and $g$ on the $B$ summand.

**Proposition 5.3 (Bifunctoriality).** The join of maps is equivariant and simplicial. It preserves identity maps and composition:

$$
\operatorname{id}_A*\operatorname{id}_B=\operatorname{id}_{A*B},
$$

and

$$
(f\circ f')*(g\circ g')=(f*g)\circ(f'*g').
$$

**Proof sketch.** Each assertion is checked independently on the two disjoint summands. Antipodes never cross from one summand to the other, so mixed pairs cause no compatibility problem.

### 5.2. Joining standard spheres

**Theorem 5.4 (Octahedral join isomorphism).** For all $m,n\ge0$,

$$
S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}*S^n_{\mathrm{oct}}
\cong S^{m+n+1}_{\mathrm{oct}}.
$$

**Proof sketch.** The first factor has coordinate labels $0,
\ldots,m$ and the second has labels $0,\ldots,n$. Relabel the first block by $0,\ldots,m$ and the second by $m+1,\ldots,m+n+1$, preserving signs. This is an equivariant bijection between two systems with $m+n+2$ antipodal orbits, and hence an equivariant simplicial isomorphism.

**Corollary 5.5 (Standard-sphere join formula).** One has

$$
\operatorname{coind}(S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}*S^n_{\mathrm{oct}})=m+n+1.
$$

In particular, joining with $S^0_{\mathrm{oct}}$ raises coindex by one.

### 5.3. Constructive lower bound

**Theorem 5.6 (Join of witnesses).** Suppose there are equivariant simplicial maps

$$
S^a_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
S^b_{\mathrm{oct}}\to L.
$$

Then there is an equivariant simplicial map

$$
S^{a+b+1}_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K*L.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Invert the isomorphism of Theorem 5.4 to map $S^{a+b+1}_{\mathrm{oct}}$ into $S^a_{\mathrm{oct}}*S^b_{\mathrm{oct}}$, then apply the join of the two given maps.

**Corollary 5.7 (Constructive coindex lower bound).** For finite nonempty $K$ and $L$,

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K)+\operatorname{coind}(L)+1
\le \operatorname{coind}(K*L).
$$

**Proof sketch.** By Theorem 3.5, the coindices of $K$ and $L$ are attained by maps from their maximal source spheres. Apply Theorem 5.6.

### 5.4. Sharp general law

**Theorem 5.8 (Sharp join law).** For all finite nonempty free $\mathbb Z_2$-sets with the octahedral simplicial structure,

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=
\operatorname{coind}(K)+\operatorname{coind}(L)+1.
$$

**Proof.** Let $K$ have $r$ antipodal orbits and $L$ have $s$. Their join has $r+s$ orbits. Corollary 4.2 gives

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=r+s-1.
$$

The same corollary gives $\operatorname{coind}(K)=r-1$ and $\operatorname{coind}(L)=s-1$. Therefore

$$
r+s-1=(r-1)+(s-1)+1.
$$

This matches the constructive lower bound and supplies the upper bound.

**Corollary 5.9 (Suspension jump).** For finite nonempty $K$,

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K*S^0_{\mathrm{oct}})=\operatorname{coind}(K)+1.
$$

**Corollary 5.10 (Commutativity and associativity at coindex level).** For finite nonempty $K,L,M$,

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=\operatorname{coind}(L*K)
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{coind}((K*L)*M)=\operatorname{coind}(K*(L*M)).
$$

**Proof sketch.** Apply Theorem 5.8 and the commutativity and associativity of addition. Explicitly, both triple joins have coindex

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K)+\operatorname{coind}(L)+\operatorname{coind}(M)+2.
$$

More generally, for $t\ge1$ finite nonempty objects $K_1,\ldots,K_t$,

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K_1*\cdots*K_t)
=
\sum_{i=1}^t\operatorname{coind}(K_i)+(t-1).
$$

## 6. Algorithms

The classification makes all principal computations linear in the number of vertices.

### 6.1. Validating an involution and computing coindex

Given a finite vertex list and a proposed antipode table, first verify that every antipode is present, that $\bar v\ne v$, and that $\bar{\bar v}=v$. Traverse unvisited vertices orbit by orbit. Each new vertex contributes exactly one pair. If the number of pairs is $r>0$, return $r-1$.

The running time is $O(N)$ expected with hash tables, where $N=|V(K)|$, and the auxiliary memory is $O(N)$. Since all valid orbits have size two, the answer is also $N/2-1$; explicit traversal is nevertheless useful for validating the input.

### 6.2. Constructing a normal-form isomorphism

Choose a deterministic representative of each orbit, for example the smaller vertex under a supplied total order. Sort these representatives. Assign the $i$th representative to $(i,+)$ and its antipode to $(i,-)$. This produces the classification isomorphism. With sorting, complexity is $O(N\log N)$; if stable input order is accepted, it is $O(N)$.

### 6.3. Forming joins

Tag vertices from $K$ as left and vertices from $L$ as right. Define the antipode without changing the tag. The resulting size is $N_K+N_L$, its orbit count is $r_K+r_L$, and its coindex may be obtained either by counting or by the sharp formula. Construction takes $O(N_K+N_L)$ time and space.

### 6.4. Validating maps

For a proposed map $f:K\to L$, check equivariance on every vertex, injectivity, and target membership. In this model, equivariance plus injectivity is sufficient for simpliciality: if $f(p)=\overline{f(q)}=f(\bar q)$, injectivity yields $p=\bar q$. The validation therefore runs in $O(N_K)$ expected time with hashing.

## 7. Numerical examples and applications

### 7.1. Exact arithmetic examples

If $K$ has $4$ orbits, then $|V(K)|=8$ and $\operatorname{coind}(K)=3$. If $L$ has $7$ orbits, then $|V(L)|=14$ and $\operatorname{coind}(L)=6$. Their join has $11$ orbits and $22$ vertices, so

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=10=3+6+1.
$$

For orbit counts $2$, $3$, and $5$, every parenthesization of the triple join has $10$ orbits and coindex $9$. This agrees with

$$
(2-1)+(3-1)+(5-1)+2=9.
$$

A target with $12$ vertices has $6$ orbits and coindex $5$. The sphere $S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}$ can map into it only when $2(m+1)\le12$, or $m\le5$. Classification shows that this bound is attained.

### 7.2. Non-compression of signed states

Suppose each orbit represents a state with two opposite orientations. An admissible encoding must preserve orientation reversal and must not make non-opposite states appear opposite. Theorem 3.1 says that such an encoding cannot merge any two states. Thus a target requires at least as many vertices and as many paired states as the source.

### 7.3. Modular composition

When two signed systems model independent modules, their join concatenates their orbit families. Theorem 5.8 gives a constant-time formula for the capacity index once the two factor indices are known. Repeated joins similarly reduce to a sum, making the invariant useful as a compositional summary.

### 7.4. Coloring-type interpretations

Associate a graph whose forbidden relationships reflect antipodal incompatibility. Injectivity supplies immediate lower bounds for symmetry-respecting labelings: no admissible equivariant map can collapse distinct vertices. The exact translation to a chromatic invariant depends on the chosen graph and coloring rule, but the orbit classification identifies the basic obstruction and suggests sharp bounds in models where colors correspond to antipodal-pair-free blocks.

## 8. Discussion and limitations

The main phenomenon is a collapse from map-theoretic complexity to cardinality. Three facts drive it: every face restriction is generated by antipodal pairs; equivariance transports a collision into an antipodal-image relation; and simpliciality converts that relation back into equality of source vertices. The first fact is special to the octahedral model.

Accordingly, Theorem 4.1 should not be read as a classification of arbitrary free simplicial $\mathbb Z_2$-complexes. If additional nonfaces are permitted, two complexes with the same vertex involution can have different topology and different equivariant mapping behavior. In richer categories, upper bounds for index-like invariants may again require cohomological or other global methods.

Nonemptiness is also essential for the stated normalization. The formula $r-1$ presupposes $r\ge1$. Rather than assign an artificial natural-number coindex to the empty object, all classification and exact join statements explicitly assume a vertex exists.

Within the intended category, however, the results are exhaustive. Coindex determines orbit count, orbit count determines isomorphism type, join adds orbit counts, and maps are injections. The shifted quantity

$$
\widehat c(K)=\operatorname{coind}(K)+1
$$

is exactly the number of antipodal orbits and is strictly additive under join:

$$
\widehat c(K*L)=\widehat c(K)+\widehat c(L).
$$

This shifted formulation reveals that the $+1$ in the unshifted join law is solely a dimension normalization.

## 9. Future work

A first direction is a weight-graded refinement. Assign a positive weight to each antipodal orbit and seek a weighted coindex whose join behavior records multiset union. The ordinary invariant is the specialization in which all weights equal one; alternative normalizations may replace the dimension shift by a minimum- or threshold-dependent correction.

A second direction concerns equivariant colorings. One may partition vertices into blocks containing no antipodal pair and require compatibility with the involution. The injectivity mechanism suggests a lower bound involving $\operatorname{coind}(K)+2$, while classification may permit exact constructions and links to Kneser-type graphs.

A third direction is axiomatic uniqueness. Consider numerical invariants of finite nonempty objects that are monotone under equivariant simplicial maps, normalized on $S^0_{\mathrm{oct}}$, and additive after the same shift under join. Since every object is a finite join of zero-spheres up to isomorphism, one expects these axioms to characterize coindex uniquely.

Further questions include automorphism groups of the normal forms, canonical representative selection, stability under controlled relaxations of the face rule, and extensions to free actions of larger finite groups. The central test for each extension is whether equivariance and local compatibility still force injectivity; if they do not, the gap between counting and topology reopens.

## 10. Conclusion

Finite octahedral $\mathbb Z_2$-complexes admit a complete and elementary structure theory. Every equivariant simplicial map is injective. Every finite nonempty object is an octahedral sphere determined by its number of antipodal orbits. Its coindex is exactly that number minus one, and the supremum defining coindex is attained. The join operation concatenates orbit families and acts functorially on maps, producing the sharp identity

$$
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=\operatorname{coind}(K)+\operatorname{coind}(L)+1.
$$

What initially appears to be an obstruction problem is therefore a classification problem, and the classification reduces the invariant to arithmetic.

\begin{abstract}
We study finite sets with a fixed-point-free involution, equipped with the octahedral simplicial structure in which faces are precisely the finite subsets containing no complete antipodal pair. An equivariant simplicial map is a vertex map commuting with the involutions and preserving this constraint. The coindex of such an object is the largest dimension of an octahedral sphere admitting an equivariant simplicial map into it. We prove that every equivariant simplicial map is vertex-injective. This gives a uniform cardinality obstruction: a map from the $m$-dimensional octahedral sphere into $K$ requires at least $2(m+1)$ vertices. We then classify every finite nonempty object as an octahedral sphere: if $K$ has $r$ antipodal orbits, then $K$ is equivariantly isomorphic to the boundary of the $r$-dimensional cross-polytope. Consequently,

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K)=r-1=\frac{|V(K)|}{2}-1.
\]

The coindex is therefore a complete invariant up to equivariant simplicial isomorphism in this model. We construct the join bifunctor, identify the join of two octahedral spheres with a sphere of dimension one greater than the sum of dimensions, and establish the sharp formula

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=\operatorname{coind}(K)+\operatorname{coind}(L)+1
\]

for all finite nonempty objects. We also prove monotonicity under equivariant simplicial maps, attainment of the defining maximum, commutativity and associativity at coindex level, and functoriality of join. Algorithms for classification, coindex computation, join formation, and map validation are provided, together with applications to non-compression, signed encodings, and coloring-type questions.

\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Antipodal symmetry is one of the simplest nontrivial group actions. A free action of $\mathbb Z_2$ partitions a set into pairs, and this pairing supports combinatorial analogues of centrally symmetric spheres. Despite the elementary data, invariants defined through equivariant maps can resemble classical topological indices and may appear to demand global obstruction theory.

The present setting is deliberately specific. Given a free $\mathbb Z_2$-set, we declare a vertex subset to be a face exactly when it avoids containing both members of any antipodal pair. This is the octahedral, or cross-polytope-boundary, structure. Its specificity creates strong rigidity: equivariance and simpliciality together force every admissible map to be injective. The resulting theory is governed entirely by the number of antipodal orbits.

Our main structural result classifies every finite nonempty object in this model. If it has $r$ orbits, it is equivariantly simplicially isomorphic to the standard octahedral sphere of dimension $r-1$. Thus the coindex, initially defined as a supremum over source spheres, is simply $r-1$. This turns the join law into orbit arithmetic. The join has the disjoint union of the two vertex sets, hence the sum of their orbit counts, and the normalization from orbit count to dimension yields the correction term $+1$.

The restriction to the octahedral simplicial structure is essential. A general free simplicial $\mathbb Z_2$-complex may have many more restrictions on its faces, and its equivariant type need not be determined by the cardinality of its vertex orbits. Here, however, all allowable faces are generated by one rule---avoid antipodal pairs---and the classification is exact.

\section{Definitions and basic constructions}

\subsection{Finite free $\mathbb Z_2$-sets}

\begin{definition}[Free involutive vertex system]
A free $\mathbb Z_2$-set $K$ consists of a vertex set $V(K)$ and a map $\alpha_K:V(K)\to V(K)$ such that, for every $v\in V(K)$,

\[
\alpha_K(\alpha_K(v))=v
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\alpha_K(v)\ne v.
\]

We write $\bar v$ for $\alpha_K(v)$. The orbits are the pairs $\{v,\bar v\}$.

\end{definition}
\begin{definition}[Octahedral simplicial structure]
The faces of $K$ are the finite subsets $\sigma\subseteq V(K)$ satisfying

\[
\text{there is no }v\text{ for which }\{v,\bar v\}\subseteq\sigma.
\]

Equivalently, a face contains at most one member of each antipodal orbit.

This convention makes every finite free involutive set into a simplicial complex without adding further data. If $K$ has $r$ orbits, its maximal faces have $r$ vertices.

\end{definition}
\subsection{Equivariant simplicial maps}

\begin{definition}[Equivariant simplicial map]
A map $f:K\to L$ is a vertex function $f:V(K)\to V(L)$ satisfying:

\noindent 1. \textbf{Equivariance:} $f(\bar v)=\overline{f(v)}$ for every $v$.\\
\noindent 2. \textbf{Simpliciality:} whenever $f(p)=\overline{f(q)}$, one has $p=\bar q$.\\

The second condition is equivalent to preservation of all antipodal-pair-free faces. Indeed, a source face could fail to map to a target face only if two non-antipodal source vertices mapped to a complete antipodal pair.

Identity maps satisfy these conditions, and composites of such maps again satisfy them. An equivariant bijection is automatically an equivariant simplicial isomorphism, since injectivity converts antipodality of images into antipodality of sources.

\end{definition}
\subsection{Standard octahedral spheres}

\begin{definition}[Octahedral sphere]
For $n\ge 0$, define

\[
S^n_{\mathrm{oct}}=\{(i,\varepsilon):0\le i\le n,\ \varepsilon\in\{+,-\}\},
\]

with antipode $\overline{(i,+)}=(i,-)$ and $\overline{(i,-)}=(i,+)$. Its simplicial structure forbids choosing both signs at a fixed coordinate.

This is the boundary complex of the $(n+1)$-dimensional cross-polytope, with signed unit vectors $\pm e_0,\ldots,\pm e_n$ as vertices.

\end{definition}
\begin{lemma}[Cardinality of the standard sphere]
The octahedral sphere $S^n_{\mathrm{oct}}$ has

\[
|V(S^n_{\mathrm{oct}})|=2(n+1)
\]

vertices and $n+1$ antipodal orbits.

\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
There are $n+1$ coordinate labels and two signs for each label.

\end{proof}
\subsection{Coindex}

\begin{definition}[Coindex]
For a free $\mathbb Z_2$-set $K$, define

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K)=
\sup\{m\in\mathbb N: S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\text{ admits an equivariant simplicial map into }K\}.
\]

For finite nonempty $K$, we shall prove that this supremum is finite, attained, and equal to the number of antipodal orbits minus one.

\end{definition}
\begin{proposition}[Maps between standard spheres]
There exists an equivariant simplicial map

\[
S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\longrightarrow S^n_{\mathrm{oct}}
\]

if and only if $m\le n$. Consequently,

\[
\operatorname{coind}(S^n_{\mathrm{oct}})=n.
\]

\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $m\le n$, include the first $m+1$ signed coordinate pairs among the $n+1$ pairs. Conversely, the injectivity theorem below forces $2(m+1)\le2(n+1)$, hence $m\le n$.

\end{proof}
\section{Rigidity and the cardinality obstruction}

\subsection{Vertex injectivity}

\begin{theorem}[Injectivity of equivariant simplicial maps]
Every equivariant simplicial map $f:K\to L$ is injective on vertices.

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $f(p)=f(q)$. Equivariance and involutivity give

\[
f(q)=\overline{f(\bar q)}.
\]

Thus $f(p)=\overline{f(\bar q)}$. By simpliciality, $p=\overline{\bar q}=q$. Therefore $f$ is injective.

This short argument is the central rigidity principle. Equivariance alone permits an entire orbit to map to another orbit, while simpliciality alone need not prevent ordinary collisions. Together they prohibit every collision.

\end{proof}
\subsection{A finite Borsuk--Ulam-type bound}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform vertex bound]
Let $K$ be finite. If there is an equivariant simplicial map $S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K$, then

\[
2(m+1)\le |V(K)|.
\]

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem 3.1, the map is injective. Lemma 2.5 gives $2(m+1)$ source vertices, all of which must have distinct images in $K$.

The terminology ``Borsuk--Ulam-type'' refers to the role of equivariance as an obstruction to mapping a larger antipodal sphere into a smaller target. In this combinatorial model, the obstruction is stronger and more elementary than a topological coincidence theorem: admissible maps are outright injections.

\end{proof}
\begin{corollary}[Boundedness]
For finite $K$, the set of integers $m$ admitting a map $S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K$ is bounded above.

\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem 3.2 implies $m+1\le |V(K)|/2$, and even the weaker bound $m\le |V(K)|$ suffices.

\end{proof}
\subsection{Attainment}

\begin{lemma}[The zero-sphere maps into every nonempty object]
If $K$ contains a vertex $v$, then there is an equivariant simplicial map $S^0_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K$ sending the two source vertices to $v$ and $\bar v$.

\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The assignment is equivariant by construction. The only antipodal image pair comes from the antipodal source pair, so it is simplicial.

\end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Attainment of coindex]
If $K$ is finite and nonempty, then an equivariant simplicial map

\[
S^{\operatorname{coind}(K)}_{\mathrm{oct}}\longrightarrow K
\]

exists.

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Lemma 3.4 makes the set in Definition 2.6 nonempty. Corollary 3.3 makes it a finite nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$, so its supremum is its maximum.

\end{proof}
\section{Classification and completeness of coindex}

\subsection{Orbit normal form}

\begin{theorem}[Classification of finite nonempty objects]
Let $K$ be a finite nonempty free $\mathbb Z_2$-set with $r$ antipodal orbits. Then $r\ge1$, and there exists an equivariant simplicial isomorphism

\[
K\cong S^{r-1}_{\mathrm{oct}}.
\]

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Choose one representative $x_i$ from each antipodal orbit and enumerate them by $i=0,\ldots,r-1$. Every vertex is uniquely either $x_i$ or $\bar x_i$. Define

\[
x_i\longmapsto(i,+),
\qquad
\bar x_i\longmapsto(i,-).
\]

This is a bijection and commutes with antipodes. Because both source and target declare exactly the antipodal-pair-free subsets to be faces, the bijection and its inverse preserve faces. Hence it is an equivariant simplicial isomorphism.

The choice of representatives is not canonical, but existence is enough for classification. Different choices change signs or permute coordinate axes, operations that are themselves automorphisms of the standard sphere.

\end{proof}
\begin{corollary}[Coindex formula]
If $K$ is finite and nonempty with $r$ antipodal orbits, then

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K)=r-1.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
2\bigl(\operatorname{coind}(K)+1\bigr)=|V(K)|.
\]

\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem 4.1, $K$ is isomorphic to $S^{r-1}_{\mathrm{oct}}$. Coindex is unchanged by equivariant simplicial isomorphism, and Proposition 2.7 gives coindex $r-1$. Since every orbit has two vertices, $|V(K)|=2r$.

\end{proof}
\begin{corollary}[Completeness]
Two finite nonempty objects $K$ and $L$ are equivariantly simplicially isomorphic if and only if

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K)=\operatorname{coind}(L).
\]

\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
An isomorphism preserves coindex. Conversely, equal coindices imply equal orbit counts by Corollary 4.2, and Theorem 4.1 identifies both objects with the same standard octahedral sphere.

Thus coindex is not merely an obstruction or a lower-dimensional shadow. Within this category it is a complete invariant.

\end{proof}
\subsection{Monotonicity}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity]
If $L$ is finite and there is an equivariant simplicial map $K\to L$, then

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K)\le\operatorname{coind}(L).
\]

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Any map $S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K$ composes with $K\to L$ to give a map $S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}\to L$. Therefore every admissible dimension for $K$ is admissible for $L$, and the supremum cannot decrease. When both objects are finite and nonempty, Theorem 3.1 gives the equivalent cardinality argument $|V(K)|\le|V(L)|$.

\end{proof}
\section{Join and its exact coindex law}

\subsection{Join of objects and maps}

\begin{definition}[Join]
The join $K*L$ has vertex set the disjoint union

\[
V(K*L)=V(K)\sqcup V(L),
\]

with the antipodal action inherited separately on each summand. Its faces are all antipodal-pair-free subsets of this disjoint union.

If $K$ and $L$ have $r$ and $s$ antipodal orbits, respectively, then $K*L$ has $r+s$ orbits.

\end{definition}
\begin{definition}[Join of maps]
Given equivariant simplicial maps $f:A\to K$ and $g:B\to L$, define

\[
f*g:A*B\longrightarrow K*L
\]

by using $f$ on the $A$ summand and $g$ on the $B$ summand.

\end{definition}
\begin{proposition}[Bifunctoriality]
The join of maps is equivariant and simplicial. It preserves identity maps and composition:

\[
\operatorname{id}_A*\operatorname{id}_B=\operatorname{id}_{A*B},
\]

and

\[
(f\circ f')*(g\circ g')=(f*g)\circ(f'*g').
\]

\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Each assertion is checked independently on the two disjoint summands. Antipodes never cross from one summand to the other, so mixed pairs cause no compatibility problem.

\end{proof}
\subsection{Joining standard spheres}

\begin{theorem}[Octahedral join isomorphism]
For all $m,n\ge0$,

\[
S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}*S^n_{\mathrm{oct}}
\cong S^{m+n+1}_{\mathrm{oct}}.
\]

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The first factor has coordinate labels $0,
\ldots,m$ and the second has labels $0,\ldots,n$. Relabel the first block by $0,\ldots,m$ and the second by $m+1,\ldots,m+n+1$, preserving signs. This is an equivariant bijection between two systems with $m+n+2$ antipodal orbits, and hence an equivariant simplicial isomorphism.

\end{proof}
\begin{corollary}[Standard-sphere join formula]
One has

\[
\operatorname{coind}(S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}*S^n_{\mathrm{oct}})=m+n+1.
\]

In particular, joining with $S^0_{\mathrm{oct}}$ raises coindex by one.

\end{corollary}
\subsection{Constructive lower bound}

\begin{theorem}[Join of witnesses]
Suppose there are equivariant simplicial maps

\[
S^a_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
S^b_{\mathrm{oct}}\to L.
\]

Then there is an equivariant simplicial map

\[
S^{a+b+1}_{\mathrm{oct}}\to K*L.
\]

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Invert the isomorphism of Theorem 5.4 to map $S^{a+b+1}_{\mathrm{oct}}$ into $S^a_{\mathrm{oct}}*S^b_{\mathrm{oct}}$, then apply the join of the two given maps.

\end{proof}
\begin{corollary}[Constructive coindex lower bound]
For finite nonempty $K$ and $L$,

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K)+\operatorname{coind}(L)+1
\le \operatorname{coind}(K*L).
\]

\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem 3.5, the coindices of $K$ and $L$ are attained by maps from their maximal source spheres. Apply Theorem 5.6.

\end{proof}
\subsection{Sharp general law}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp join law]
For all finite nonempty free $\mathbb Z_2$-sets with the octahedral simplicial structure,

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=
\operatorname{coind}(K)+\operatorname{coind}(L)+1.
\]

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $K$ have $r$ antipodal orbits and $L$ have $s$. Their join has $r+s$ orbits. Corollary 4.2 gives

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=r+s-1.
\]

The same corollary gives $\operatorname{coind}(K)=r-1$ and $\operatorname{coind}(L)=s-1$. Therefore

\[
r+s-1=(r-1)+(s-1)+1.
\]

This matches the constructive lower bound and supplies the upper bound.

\end{proof}
\begin{corollary}[Suspension jump]
For finite nonempty $K$,

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K*S^0_{\mathrm{oct}})=\operatorname{coind}(K)+1.
\]

\end{corollary}
\begin{corollary}[Commutativity and associativity at coindex level]
For finite nonempty $K,L,M$,

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=\operatorname{coind}(L*K)
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{coind}((K*L)*M)=\operatorname{coind}(K*(L*M)).
\]

\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem 5.8 and the commutativity and associativity of addition. Explicitly, both triple joins have coindex

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K)+\operatorname{coind}(L)+\operatorname{coind}(M)+2.
\]

More generally, for $t\ge1$ finite nonempty objects $K_1,\ldots,K_t$,

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K_1*\cdots*K_t)
=
\sum_{i=1}^t\operatorname{coind}(K_i)+(t-1).
\]

\end{proof}
\section{Algorithms}

The classification makes all principal computations linear in the number of vertices.

\subsection{Validating an involution and computing coindex}

Given a finite vertex list and a proposed antipode table, first verify that every antipode is present, that $\bar v\ne v$, and that $\bar{\bar v}=v$. Traverse unvisited vertices orbit by orbit. Each new vertex contributes exactly one pair. If the number of pairs is $r>0$, return $r-1$.

The running time is $O(N)$ expected with hash tables, where $N=|V(K)|$, and the auxiliary memory is $O(N)$. Since all valid orbits have size two, the answer is also $N/2-1$; explicit traversal is nevertheless useful for validating the input.

\subsection{Constructing a normal-form isomorphism}

Choose a deterministic representative of each orbit, for example the smaller vertex under a supplied total order. Sort these representatives. Assign the $i$th representative to $(i,+)$ and its antipode to $(i,-)$. This produces the classification isomorphism. With sorting, complexity is $O(N\log N)$; if stable input order is accepted, it is $O(N)$.

\subsection{Forming joins}

Tag vertices from $K$ as left and vertices from $L$ as right. Define the antipode without changing the tag. The resulting size is $N_K+N_L$, its orbit count is $r_K+r_L$, and its coindex may be obtained either by counting or by the sharp formula. Construction takes $O(N_K+N_L)$ time and space.

\subsection{Validating maps}

For a proposed map $f:K\to L$, check equivariance on every vertex, injectivity, and target membership. In this model, equivariance plus injectivity is sufficient for simpliciality: if $f(p)=\overline{f(q)}=f(\bar q)$, injectivity yields $p=\bar q$. The validation therefore runs in $O(N_K)$ expected time with hashing.

\section{Numerical examples and applications}

\subsection{Exact arithmetic examples}

If $K$ has $4$ orbits, then $|V(K)|=8$ and $\operatorname{coind}(K)=3$. If $L$ has $7$ orbits, then $|V(L)|=14$ and $\operatorname{coind}(L)=6$. Their join has $11$ orbits and $22$ vertices, so

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=10=3+6+1.
\]

For orbit counts $2$, $3$, and $5$, every parenthesization of the triple join has $10$ orbits and coindex $9$. This agrees with

\[
(2-1)+(3-1)+(5-1)+2=9.
\]

A target with $12$ vertices has $6$ orbits and coindex $5$. The sphere $S^m_{\mathrm{oct}}$ can map into it only when $2(m+1)\le12$, or $m\le5$. Classification shows that this bound is attained.

\subsection{Non-compression of signed states}

Suppose each orbit represents a state with two opposite orientations. An admissible encoding must preserve orientation reversal and must not make non-opposite states appear opposite. Theorem 3.1 says that such an encoding cannot merge any two states. Thus a target requires at least as many vertices and as many paired states as the source.

\subsection{Modular composition}

When two signed systems model independent modules, their join concatenates their orbit families. Theorem 5.8 gives a constant-time formula for the capacity index once the two factor indices are known. Repeated joins similarly reduce to a sum, making the invariant useful as a compositional summary.

\subsection{Coloring-type interpretations}

Associate a graph whose forbidden relationships reflect antipodal incompatibility. Injectivity supplies immediate lower bounds for symmetry-respecting labelings: no admissible equivariant map can collapse distinct vertices. The exact translation to a chromatic invariant depends on the chosen graph and coloring rule, but the orbit classification identifies the basic obstruction and suggests sharp bounds in models where colors correspond to antipodal-pair-free blocks.

\section{Discussion and limitations}

The main phenomenon is a collapse from map-theoretic complexity to cardinality. Three facts drive it: every face restriction is generated by antipodal pairs; equivariance transports a collision into an antipodal-image relation; and simpliciality converts that relation back into equality of source vertices. The first fact is special to the octahedral model.

Accordingly, Theorem 4.1 should not be read as a classification of arbitrary free simplicial $\mathbb Z_2$-complexes. If additional nonfaces are permitted, two complexes with the same vertex involution can have different topology and different equivariant mapping behavior. In richer categories, upper bounds for index-like invariants may again require cohomological or other global methods.

Nonemptiness is also essential for the stated normalization. The formula $r-1$ presupposes $r\ge1$. Rather than assign an artificial natural-number coindex to the empty object, all classification and exact join statements explicitly assume a vertex exists.

Within the intended category, however, the results are exhaustive. Coindex determines orbit count, orbit count determines isomorphism type, join adds orbit counts, and maps are injections. The shifted quantity

\[
\widehat c(K)=\operatorname{coind}(K)+1
\]

is exactly the number of antipodal orbits and is strictly additive under join:

\[
\widehat c(K*L)=\widehat c(K)+\widehat c(L).
\]

This shifted formulation reveals that the $+1$ in the unshifted join law is solely a dimension normalization.

\section{Future work}

A first direction is a weight-graded refinement. Assign a positive weight to each antipodal orbit and seek a weighted coindex whose join behavior records multiset union. The ordinary invariant is the specialization in which all weights equal one; alternative normalizations may replace the dimension shift by a minimum- or threshold-dependent correction.

A second direction concerns equivariant colorings. One may partition vertices into blocks containing no antipodal pair and require compatibility with the involution. The injectivity mechanism suggests a lower bound involving $\operatorname{coind}(K)+2$, while classification may permit exact constructions and links to Kneser-type graphs.

A third direction is axiomatic uniqueness. Consider numerical invariants of finite nonempty objects that are monotone under equivariant simplicial maps, normalized on $S^0_{\mathrm{oct}}$, and additive after the same shift under join. Since every object is a finite join of zero-spheres up to isomorphism, one expects these axioms to characterize coindex uniquely.

Further questions include automorphism groups of the normal forms, canonical representative selection, stability under controlled relaxations of the face rule, and extensions to free actions of larger finite groups. The central test for each extension is whether equivariance and local compatibility still force injectivity; if they do not, the gap between counting and topology reopens.

\section{Conclusion}

Finite octahedral $\mathbb Z_2$-complexes admit a complete and elementary structure theory. Every equivariant simplicial map is injective. Every finite nonempty object is an octahedral sphere determined by its number of antipodal orbits. Its coindex is exactly that number minus one, and the supremum defining coindex is attained. The join operation concatenates orbit families and acts functorially on maps, producing the sharp identity

\[
\operatorname{coind}(K*L)=\operatorname{coind}(K)+\operatorname{coind}(L)+1.
\]

What initially appears to be an obstruction problem is therefore a classification problem, and the classification reduces the invariant to arithmetic.

"""Numerical demonstrations of coindex classification and the sharp join law."""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, Hashable, Iterable, Mapping, Sequence, Tuple, TypeVar

Vertex = TypeVar("Vertex", bound=Hashable)
TaggedVertex = Tuple[str, Hashable]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FreeZ2Set:
    """A finite vertex system represented by its fixed-point-free involution."""

    antipode: Mapping[Hashable, Hashable]

    def validate(self) -> None:
        """Raise ValueError unless the table is a fixed-point-free involution."""
        vertices = set(self.antipode)
        for vertex, opposite in self.antipode.items():
            if opposite not in vertices:
                raise ValueError(f"antipode {opposite!r} is not a vertex")
            if opposite == vertex:
                raise ValueError(f"fixed point at {vertex!r}")
            if self.antipode[opposite] != vertex:
                raise ValueError(f"involution law fails at {vertex!r}")

    @property
    def vertices(self) -> frozenset[Hashable]:
        self.validate()
        return frozenset(self.antipode)

    def orbits(self) -> Tuple[frozenset[Hashable], ...]:
        """Return the antipodal pairs in deterministic display order."""
        self.validate()
        unseen = set(self.antipode)
        pairs = []
        while unseen:
            vertex = min(unseen, key=repr)
            opposite = self.antipode[vertex]
            pair = frozenset((vertex, opposite))
            pairs.append(pair)
            unseen.difference_update(pair)
        return tuple(pairs)

    def coindex(self) -> int:
        """Compute orbit count minus one; the object must be nonempty."""
        orbit_count = len(self.orbits())
        if orbit_count == 0:
            raise ValueError("coindex formula requires a nonempty object")
        return orbit_count - 1


def octahedral_sphere(dimension: int, prefix: str = "x") -> FreeZ2Set:
    """Build the signed coordinate model of the octahedral dimension sphere."""
    if dimension < 0:
        raise ValueError("dimension must be nonnegative")
    table: Dict[Hashable, Hashable] = {}
    for axis in range(dimension + 1):
        positive = f"+{prefix}{axis}"
        negative = f"-{prefix}{axis}"
        table[positive] = negative
        table[negative] = positive
    return FreeZ2Set(table)


def from_orbit_count(count: int, prefix: str) -> FreeZ2Set:
    """Construct a normal-form object with the requested number of orbits."""
    if count <= 0:
        raise ValueError("a nonempty object needs at least one orbit")
    return octahedral_sphere(count - 1, prefix)


def join(left: FreeZ2Set, right: FreeZ2Set) -> FreeZ2Set:
    """Form the disjoint-union join, tagging each summand."""
    left.validate()
    right.validate()
    table: Dict[Hashable, Hashable] = {}
    for vertex, opposite in left.antipode.items():
        table[("L", vertex)] = ("L", opposite)
    for vertex, opposite in right.antipode.items():
        table[("R", vertex)] = ("R", opposite)
    return FreeZ2Set(table)


def validate_equivariant_map(
    source: FreeZ2Set,
    target: FreeZ2Set,
    mapping: Mapping[Hashable, Hashable],
) -> bool:
    """Test totality, target membership, equivariance, and injectivity."""
    source.validate()
    target.validate()
    if set(mapping) != set(source.antipode):
        return False
    if any(image not in target.antipode for image in mapping.values()):
        return False
    if len(set(mapping.values())) != len(mapping):
        return False
    return all(
        mapping[source.antipode[v]] == target.antipode[mapping[v]]
        for v in source.antipode
    )


def sphere_embedding(source_dimension: int, target: FreeZ2Set) -> Dict[Hashable, Hashable]:
    """Construct an embedding from a standard sphere when the vertex bound allows it."""
    source = octahedral_sphere(source_dimension, "s")
    target_pairs = target.orbits()
    if source_dimension + 1 > len(target_pairs):
        raise ValueError("vertex bound forbids this embedding")
    mapping: Dict[Hashable, Hashable] = {}
    for axis, pair in enumerate(target_pairs[: source_dimension + 1]):
        first = min(pair, key=repr)
        second = target.antipode[first]
        mapping[f"+s{axis}"] = first
        mapping[f"-s{axis}"] = second
    assert validate_equivariant_map(source, target, mapping)
    return mapping

  "future_directions": "# Future Directions: the coindex as a complete combinatorial invariant

This cycle closed the gap between the two halves of the join law for the ℤ₂-coindex of free ℤ₂-sets. The lower half (a constructive, join-of-witnesses argument) was already known; the upper half was believed to require an equivariant cohomological obstruction. We showed instead that, in the octahedral combinatorial model, the coindex is a **complete invariant** of a finite free ℤ₂-set — it equals the number of antipodal orbits minus one — so the sharp join law `coind(K ⋆ L) = coind(K) + coind(L) + 1` holds for *all* finite nonempty free ℤ₂-sets. The following conjectures push this classification principle further.

## 1. A weight-graded refinement of the join law

**Conjecture.** Assign to each antipodal orbit a positive integer weight and define a weighted coindex by counting weighted orbits. Then the weighted coindex is additive under join with an explicit correction term determined only by the multiset of weights, generalizing the `+1` shift to a `+min`-type law.

*The key insight is* that the ordinary join law is the weight-one specialization of an additive law on the free commutative monoid of orbit-weight multisets, so the `+1` is really the size of the smallest new simplex created by joining.

*The key insight is* that vertex injectivity of equivariant simplicial maps — the mechanism behind the upper bound proved this cycle — is precisely what forbids collapsing antipodal orbits, which is the combinatorial content of a coloring lower bound.

*Why now?* The completeness of the coindex invariant means such colorability statements can be reduced to pure orbit arithmetic, removing the topological detour used in classical proofs.

## 3. Functorial rigidity of the coindex on the join-monoid

**Conjecture.** The coindex is the unique monoid homomorphism (up to the shift normalization) from the join-monoid of finite free ℤ₂-sets to `(ℕ, +)` that is monotone under equivariant maps and normalized on the zero-sphere. *The key insight is* that monotonicity under equivariant maps plus additivity under join pins down a single numerical invariant once its value on the generator `S⁰` is fixed.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, Hashable, Iterable, Mapping, Sequence, Tuple, TypeVar

Vertex = TypeVar("Vertex", bound=Hashable)
TaggedVertex = Tuple[str, Hashable]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FreeZ2Set:
    """A finite vertex system represented by its fixed-point-free involution."""

    antipode: Mapping[Hashable, Hashable]

    def validate(self) -> None:
        """Raise ValueError unless the table is a fixed-point-free involution."""
        vertices = set(self.antipode)
        for vertex, opposite in self.antipode.items():
            if opposite not in vertices:
                raise ValueError(f"antipode {opposite!r} is not a vertex")
            if opposite == vertex:
                raise ValueError(f"fixed point at {vertex!r}")
            if self.antipode[opposite] != vertex:
                raise ValueError(f"involution law fails at {vertex!r}")

    @property
    def vertices(self) -> frozenset[Hashable]:
        self.validate()
        return frozenset(self.antipode)

    def orbits(self) -> Tuple[frozenset[Hashable], ...]:
        """Return the antipodal pairs in deterministic display order."""
        self.validate()
        unseen = set(self.antipode)
        pairs = []
        while unseen:
            vertex = min(unseen, key=repr)
            opposite = self.antipode[vertex]
            pair = frozenset((vertex, opposite))
            pairs.append(pair)
            unseen.difference_update(pair)
        return tuple(pairs)

    def coindex(self) -> int:
        """Compute orbit count minus one; the object must be nonempty."""
        orbit_count = len(self.orbits())
        if orbit_count == 0:
            raise ValueError("coindex formula requires a nonempty object")
        return orbit_count - 1


def octahedral_sphere(dimension: int, prefix: str = "x") -> FreeZ2Set:
    """Build the signed coordinate model of the octahedral dimension sphere."""
    if dimension < 0:
        raise ValueError("dimension must be nonnegative")
    table: Dict[Hashable, Hashable] = {}
    for axis in range(dimension + 1):
        positive = f"+{prefix}{axis}"
        negative = f"-{prefix}{axis}"
        table[positive] = negative
        table[negative] = positive
    return FreeZ2Set(table)


def from_orbit_count(count: int, prefix: str) -> FreeZ2Set:
    """Construct a normal-form object with the requested number of orbits."""
    if count <= 0:
        raise ValueError("a nonempty object needs at least one orbit")
    return octahedral_sphere(count - 1, prefix)


def join(left: FreeZ2Set, right: FreeZ2Set) -> FreeZ2Set:
    """Form the disjoint-union join, tagging each summand."""
    left.validate()
    right.validate()
    table: Dict[Hashable, Hashable] = {}
    for vertex, opposite in left.antipode.items():
        table[("L", vertex)] = ("L", opposite)
    for vertex, opposite in right.antipode.items():
        table[("R", vertex)] = ("R", opposite)
    return FreeZ2Set(table)


def validate_equivariant_map(
    source: FreeZ2Set,
    target: FreeZ2Set,
    mapping: Mapping[Hashable, Hashable],
) -> bool:
    """Test totality, target membership, equivariance, and injectivity."""
    source.validate()
    target.validate()
    if set(mapping) != set(source.antipode):
        return False
    if any(image not in target.antipode for image in mapping.values()):
        return False
    if len(set(mapping.values())) != len(mapping):
        return False
    return all(
        mapping[source.antipode[v]] == target.antipode[mapping[v]]
        for v in source.antipode
    )

    """Construct an embedding from a standard sphere when the vertex bound allows it."""
    source = octahedral_sphere(source_dimension, "s")
    target_pairs = target.orbits()
    if source_dimension + 1 > len(target_pairs):
        raise ValueError("vertex bound forbids this embedding")
    mapping: Dict[Hashable, Hashable] = {}
    for axis, pair in enumerate(target_pairs[: source_dimension + 1]):
        first = min(pair, key=repr)
        second = target.antipode[first]
        mapping[f"+s{axis}"] = first
        mapping[f"-s{axis}"] = second

    return mapping

    """Print exact numerical instances of the classification and join theorem."""

    for r, s in orbit_pairs:

        right = from_orbit_count(s, "b")
        product = join(left, right)
        rhs = left.coindex() + right.coindex() + 1

            f" {len(product.vertices):13d} | {product.coindex():7d} | {rhs:3d}"

        assert product.coindex() == rhs
        assert 2 * (product.coindex() + 1) == len(product.vertices)

            f"embedding constructed={constructed}"
        )
        assert constructed == bound

    """Compare both parenthesizations for three nonempty factors."""

    print(f"sum formula={expected}")
    assert left.coindex() == right.coindex() == expected

    demonstrate_vertex_bound(6)
    demonstrate_associativity((2, 3, 5))


if __name__ == "__main__":

# Time-Travel Logic II: Recurrence, Parity, and Coordinate-Invariance of Causal Loops

A second layer on the theory of closed timelike curves (CTCs) and the Novikov
self-consistency principle.  The first development modelled a causal loop by its
*loop map* `evolve : S → S` — the net effect of one traversal of a closed
timelike curve — and identified self-consistency with the existence of a fixed
point, giving positive guarantees (monotone loops via Knaster–Tarski, continuous
loops on the unit phase interval via the intermediate value theorem, involutive
loops of odd order).

Here we go deeper along four independent axes, each a genuinely new structural
principle for causal loops:

* **Coordinate invariance** (`selfConsistent_conj`): self-consistency is a
  property of the loop *up to change of world-coordinates*.  A relabelling of the
  state space by a bijection cannot create or destroy a consistent history.  This
  is the statement that the Novikov principle is intrinsic, not an artefact of a
  choice of coordinates.

* **Composability** (`selfConsistent_prod`): a loop acting independently on two
  decoupled subsystems is self-consistent exactly when each subsystem is, so
  consistency is compositional across a product world.

* **Discrete recurrence** (`loop_recurrent`, `loop_universally_consistent`): on a
  *finite* phase space every invertible loop is recurrent — each world-state
  returns to itself after finitely many traversals — and, more strongly, a single
  number of traversals `N` returns *every* state simultaneously.  This is a
  discrete Poincaré recurrence theorem: even a paradoxical loop, iterated enough
  times, becomes universally self-consistent.  It bridges the fixed-point picture
  with finite group theory (the order of the induced permutation).

* **A parity law for time-reversal loops** (`involution_fixedPoints_parity`): for
  an involutive loop (traversing twice restores the world) on a finite phase
  space, the number of self-consistent states has the *same parity* as the size
  of the phase space — a Lefschetz-style mod-2 index.  The odd-order guarantee of
  the first development is the immediate corollary that an odd phase space forces
  at least one consistent history.

The analytic guarantee is also sharpened from the unit interval to an arbitrary
compact phase interval `[a,b]` (`continuous_selfConsistent_Icc`).

The four axes converge on the grandfather paradox: it is fixed-point-free
(`grandfather_paradoxical`), yet on the two-state phase space it is recurrent with
period two (`grandfather_recurrent`), so *two* traversals of the grandfather loop
are universally self-consistent — the multiverse is not needed to tame a paradox,
only patience.
-/

import Mathlib

namespace TimeTravelDeep

open Function

variable {S : Type*}

/-! ## Core model (recalled)

A **causal loop** is recorded by its loop map `evolve : S → S`; the loop is
*self-consistent* when some world-state is reproduced by one traversal. -/

/-- A **causal loop** (closed timelike curve): `evolve s` is the world-state that
results from feeding the state `s` once around the loop. -/
structure CausalLoop (S : Type*) where
  /-- The net effect of one traversal of the loop on the world-state. -/
  evolve : S → S

/-- **Novikov self-consistency principle.** A loop is self-consistent when some
world-state is reproduced by one traversal, i.e. a history compatible with itself. -/
def SelfConsistent (L : CausalLoop S) : Prop := ∃ s, L.evolve s = s

/-- The **iterated loop**: traversing the loop `n` times in succession. -/
def iterate (L : CausalLoop S) (n : ℕ) : CausalLoop S := ⟨L.evolve^[n]⟩

@[simp] theorem iterate_evolve (L : CausalLoop S) (n : ℕ) :
    (iterate L n).evolve = L.evolve^[n] := rfl

/-- A loop map is **paradoxical** if no world-state is left unchanged: every
history contradicts itself (the grandfather situation). -/
def Paradoxical (f : S → S) : Prop := ∀ s, f s ≠ s

/-! ## Coordinate invariance

Self-consistency is intrinsic to the loop: it survives any bijective relabelling
of the world-states. -/

/-- **Coordinate invariance of the Novikov principle.** Transporting a loop map
`f` along a bijective change of world-coordinates `e : S ≃ T` neither creates nor
destroys a self-consistent history. -/
theorem selfConsistent_conj {T : Type*} (e : S ≃ T) (f : S → S) :
    SelfConsistent (⟨f⟩ : CausalLoop S) ↔
      SelfConsistent (⟨e ∘ f ∘ e.symm⟩ : CausalLoop T) := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨s, hs⟩
    refine ⟨e s, ?_⟩
    simp only [comp_apply, Equiv.symm_apply_apply]
    exact congrArg e hs
  · rintro ⟨t, ht⟩
    refine ⟨e.symm t, ?_⟩
    have he : e (f (e.symm t)) = t := by simpa [comp_apply] using ht
    have h2 := congrArg e.symm he
    simpa using h2

/-! ## Composability across a product world -/

/-- **Compositional consistency.** A loop acting independently on two decoupled
subsystems is self-consistent exactly when both subsystems are. -/
theorem selfConsistent_prod {T : Type*} (f : S → S) (g : T → T) :
    SelfConsistent (⟨fun p => (f p.1, g p.2)⟩ : CausalLoop (S × T)) ↔
      SelfConsistent (⟨f⟩ : CausalLoop S) ∧ SelfConsistent (⟨g⟩ : CausalLoop T) := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨⟨a, b⟩, hab⟩
    simp only [Prod.mk.injEq] at hab
    exact ⟨⟨a, hab.1⟩, ⟨b, hab.2⟩⟩
  · rintro ⟨⟨a, ha⟩, ⟨b, hb⟩⟩
    exact ⟨(a, b), Prod.ext ha hb⟩

/-! ## Discrete Poincaré recurrence on a finite phase space -/

/-- **Universal recurrence.** On a finite phase space, an invertible loop returns
*every* world-state to itself after one common number `N > 0` of traversals: the
`N`-fold iterated loop is the identity. Equivalently, iterated enough times, any
invertible causal loop becomes universally self-consistent. -/
theorem loop_universally_consistent [Finite S] [Nonempty S] (f : S → S)
    (hf : Bijective f) : ∃ N, 0 < N ∧ ∀ s, f^[N] s = s := by
  classical
  cases nonempty_fintype S

  have hfix : (⇑σ)^[orderOf σ] s = s := by rw [← h2, h1]; rfl
  simpa [σ, Equiv.ofBijective] using hfix

/-- **Discrete Poincaré recurrence.** Every world-state of an invertible loop on a

# Future Directions: Recurrence and Symmetry in the Logic of Causal Loops

This cycle deepened the theory of closed timelike curves beyond the bare
fixed-point (Novikov self-consistency) picture, establishing four independent
structural principles for a causal loop presented by its loop map: coordinate
invariance, product compositionality, discrete recurrence on finite phase spaces,
and a parity law for time-reversal loops. The following conjectures push each of
these frontiers.

## 1. Uniform recurrence time and the spectrum of return periods

**Conjecture.** For an invertible loop on a finite phase space, the set of return
periods of individual world-states is exactly the set of divisors of a single
universal period, and the minimal universal period equals the least common
multiple of the individual return times.

*The key insight is* that an invertible loop on a finite world decomposes into
disjoint cyclic orbits, so the global return structure is governed entirely by the
arithmetic of orbit lengths — recurrence is a number-theoretic phenomenon, not an
analytic one.

*Why now?* The discrete recurrence principle established this cycle shows that a
single universal period exists; the natural next step is to pin down its exact
value and to characterise which states share which periods, turning a qualitative
recurrence statement into a quantitative spectral one.

## 2. A signed Lefschetz index for general loops

**Conjecture.** For every invertible loop on a finite phase space there is an
integer-valued index, computable from the orbit structure, whose parity coincides
with the number of self-consistent states, and which reduces to the phase-space
size for time-reversal loops.

*The key insight is* that the mod-2 parity law for involutions is the shadow of a
finer integer invariant: counting orbits with sign recovers a Lefschetz-type
fixed-point index that constrains consistent histories for arbitrary loops, not
only self-inverse ones.

*Why now?* This cycle proved the involutive case exactly (fixed-point count equals
phase-space size mod 2). Generalising from involutions to arbitrary invertible

# Time-Travel Logic II: Recurrence, Parity, and Coordinate-Invariance of Causal Loops

A second layer on the theory of closed timelike curves (CTCs) and the Novikov
self-consistency principle.  The first development modelled a causal loop by its
*loop map* `evolve : S → S` — the net effect of one traversal of a closed
timelike curve — and identified self-consistency with the existence of a fixed
point, giving positive guarantees (monotone loops via Knaster–Tarski, continuous
loops on the unit phase interval via the intermediate value theorem, involutive
loops of odd order).

Here we go deeper along four independent axes, each a genuinely new structural
principle for causal loops:

* **Coordinate invariance** (`selfConsistent_conj`): self-consistency is a
  property of the loop *up to change of world-coordinates*.  A relabelling of the
  state space by a bijection cannot create or destroy a consistent history.  This
  is the statement that the Novikov principle is intrinsic, not an artefact of a
  choice of coordinates.

* **Composability** (`selfConsistent_prod`): a loop acting independently on two
  decoupled subsystems is self-consistent exactly when each subsystem is, so
  consistency is compositional across a product world.

* **Discrete recurrence** (`loop_recurrent`, `loop_universally_consistent`): on a
  *finite* phase space every invertible loop is recurrent — each world-state
  returns to itself after finitely many traversals — and, more strongly, a single
  number of traversals `N` returns *every* state simultaneously.  This is a
  discrete Poincaré recurrence theorem: even a paradoxical loop, iterated enough
  times, becomes universally self-consistent.  It bridges the fixed-point picture
  with finite group theory (the order of the induced permutation).

* **A parity law for time-reversal loops** (`involution_fixedPoints_parity`): for
  an involutive loop (traversing twice restores the world) on a finite phase
  space, the number of self-consistent states has the *same parity* as the size
  of the phase space — a Lefschetz-style mod-2 index.  The odd-order guarantee of
  the first development is the immediate corollary that an odd phase space forces
  at least one consistent history.

The analytic guarantee is also sharpened from the unit interval to an arbitrary
compact phase interval `[a,b]` (`continuous_selfConsistent_Icc`).

The four axes converge on the grandfather paradox: it is fixed-point-free
(`grandfather_paradoxical`), yet on the two-state phase space it is recurrent with
period two (`grandfather_recurrent`), so *two* traversals of the grandfather loop
are universally self-consistent — the multiverse is not needed to tame a paradox,
only patience.
-/

import Mathlib

namespace TimeTravelDeep

open Function

variable {S : Type*}

/-! ## Core model (recalled)

A **causal loop** is recorded by its loop map `evolve : S → S`; the loop is
*self-consistent* when some world-state is reproduced by one traversal. -/

/-- A **causal loop** (closed timelike curve): `evolve s` is the world-state that
results from feeding the state `s` once around the loop. -/
structure CausalLoop (S : Type*) where
  /-- The net effect of one traversal of the loop on the world-state. -/
  evolve : S → S

/-- **Novikov self-consistency principle.** A loop is self-consistent when some
world-state is reproduced by one traversal, i.e. a history compatible with itself. -/
def SelfConsistent (L : CausalLoop S) : Prop := ∃ s, L.evolve s = s

/-- The **iterated loop**: traversing the loop `n` times in succession. -/
def iterate (L : CausalLoop S) (n : ℕ) : CausalLoop S := ⟨L.evolve^[n]⟩

@[simp] theorem iterate_evolve (L : CausalLoop S) (n : ℕ) :
    (iterate L n).evolve = L.evolve^[n] := rfl

/-- A loop map is **paradoxical** if no world-state is left unchanged: every
history contradicts itself (the grandfather situation). -/
def Paradoxical (f : S → S) : Prop := ∀ s, f s ≠ s

/-! ## Coordinate invariance

Self-consistency is intrinsic to the loop: it survives any bijective relabelling
of the world-states. -/

/-- **Coordinate invariance of the Novikov principle.** Transporting a loop map
`f` along a bijective change of world-coordinates `e : S ≃ T` neither creates nor
destroys a self-consistent history. -/
theorem selfConsistent_conj {T : Type*} (e : S ≃ T) (f : S → S) :
    SelfConsistent (⟨f⟩ : CausalLoop S) ↔
      SelfConsistent (⟨e ∘ f ∘ e.symm⟩ : CausalLoop T) := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨s, hs⟩
    refine ⟨e s, ?_⟩
    simp only [comp_apply, Equiv.symm_apply_apply]
    exact congrArg e hs
  · rintro ⟨t, ht⟩
    refine ⟨e.symm t, ?_⟩
    have he : e (f (e.symm t)) = t := by simpa [comp_apply] using ht
    have h2 := congrArg e.symm he
    simpa using h2

/-! ## Composability across a product world -/

/-- **Compositional consistency.** A loop acting independently on two decoupled
subsystems is self-consistent exactly when both subsystems are. -/
theorem selfConsistent_prod {T : Type*} (f : S → S) (g : T → T) :
    SelfConsistent (⟨fun p => (f p.1, g p.2)⟩ : CausalLoop (S × T)) ↔
      SelfConsistent (⟨f⟩ : CausalLoop S) ∧ SelfConsistent (⟨g⟩ : CausalLoop T) := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨⟨a, b⟩, hab⟩
    simp only [Prod.mk.injEq] at hab
    exact ⟨⟨a, hab.1⟩, ⟨b, hab.2⟩⟩
  · rintro ⟨⟨a, ha⟩, ⟨b, hb⟩⟩
    exact ⟨(a, b), Prod.ext ha hb⟩

/-! ## Discrete Poincaré recurrence on a finite phase space -/

/-- **Universal recurrence.** On a finite phase space, an invertible loop returns
*every* world-state to itself after one common number `N > 0` of traversals: the
`N`-fold iterated loop is the identity. Equivalently, iterated enough times, any
invertible causal loop becomes universally self-consistent. -/
theorem loop_universally_consistent [Finite S] [Nonempty S] (f : S → S)
    (hf : Bijective f) : ∃ N, 0 < N ∧ ∀ s, f^[N] s = s := by
  classical
  cases nonempty_fintype S
  let σ : Equiv.Perm S := Equiv.ofBijective f hf
  refine ⟨orderOf σ, orderOf_pos σ, fun s => ?_⟩
  have h1 : σ ^ orderOf σ = 1 := pow_orderOf_eq_one σ
  have h2 : ⇑(σ ^ orderOf σ) = (⇑σ)^[orderOf σ] := Equiv.Perm.coe_pow σ (orderOf σ)
  have hfix : (⇑σ)^[orderOf σ] s = s := by rw [← h2, h1]; rfl
  simpa [σ, Equiv.ofBijective] using hfix

/-- **Discrete Poincaré recurrence.** Every world-state of an invertible loop on a
finite phase space returns to itself after finitely many (positive) traversals. -/
theorem loop_recurrent [Finite S] (f : S → S) (hf : Bijective f) (s : S) :
    ∃ k, 0 < k ∧ f^[k] s = s := by
  haveI : Nonempty S := ⟨s⟩
  obtain ⟨N, hN, h⟩ := loop_universally_consistent f hf
  exact ⟨N, hN, h s⟩

/-- A packaged form: on a nonempty finite phase space, some positive iterate of an
invertible loop is self-consistent — indeed it fixes every state. -/
theorem iterate_selfConsistent_of_bijective [Finite S] [Nonempty S] (f : S → S)
    (hf : Bijective f) : ∃ N, 0 < N ∧ SelfConsistent (iterate ⟨f⟩ N) := by
  obtain ⟨N, hN, h⟩ := loop_universally_consistent f hf
  obtain ⟨s⟩ := (inferInstance : Nonempty S)
  exact ⟨N, hN, s, h s⟩

/-! ## A parity law for time-reversal (involutive) loops -/

/-- **Parity law for time-reversal loops.** For an involutive loop on a finite
phase space (traversing twice restores the world), the number of self-consistent
world-states has the same parity as the size of the phase space. This is a
Lefschetz-style mod-2 fixed-point index. -/
theorem involution_fixedPoints_parity [Fintype S] [DecidableEq S] (f : S → S)
    (hf : Involutive f) :
    Fintype.card {s // f s = s} % 2 = Fintype.card S % 2 := by
  classical
  let σ : Equiv.Perm S := Equiv.ofBijective f hf.bijective
  have hσ2 : σ ^ 2 = 1 := by
    ext x; simp only [Equiv.Perm.coe_pow, Equiv.Perm.coe_one, id_eq]; exact hf x
  have hsupp : 2 ∣ σ.support.card := Equiv.Perm.two_dvd_card_support hσ2
  have hσf : ∀ x, σ x = f x := fun x => rfl
  have hcard : Fintype.card {s // f s = s}
      = (Finset.univ.filter (fun s => f s = s)).card := by simp [Fintype.card_subtype]
  have hpart : (Finset.univ.filter (fun s => f s = s)).card + σ.support.card
      = Fintype.card S := by
    have hs : σ.support = Finset.univ.filter (fun s => ¬ (f s = s)) := by
      ext x
      simp only [Equiv.Perm.mem_support, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, hσf]
    rw [hs, Finset.card_filter_add_card_filter_not, Finset.card_univ]
  omega

/-- **Odd phase spaces force consistency** (a corollary of the parity law): an
involutive loop on a phase space of odd size is self-consistent. -/
theorem involutive_odd_selfConsistent [Fintype S] [DecidableEq S] (f : S → S)
    (hf : Involutive f) (hodd : Odd (Fintype.card S)) :
    SelfConsistent (⟨f⟩ : CausalLoop S) := by
  have hpar := involution_fixedPoints_parity f hf
  rw [Nat.odd_iff] at hodd
  rw [hodd] at hpar
  have hpos : 0 < Fintype.card {s // f s = s} := by omega
  obtain ⟨⟨s, hs⟩⟩ := Fintype.card_pos_iff.mp hpos
  exact ⟨s, hs⟩

/-! ## Sharpened analytic guarantee on an arbitrary phase interval -/

/-- **Continuous loops on a compact phase interval are self-consistent.**
Sharpening the unit-interval guarantee: any continuous loop map of an arbitrary
compact phase interval `[a,b]` into itself has a self-consistent state, by the
intermediate value theorem (1-D Brouwer). -/
theorem continuous_selfConsistent_Icc (a b : ℝ) (hab : a ≤ b) (f : ℝ → ℝ)
    (hf : ContinuousOn f (Set.Icc a b))
    (hmaps : Set.MapsTo f (Set.Icc a b) (Set.Icc a b)) :
    ∃ s ∈ Set.Icc a b, f s = s := by
  set g : ℝ → ℝ := fun x => f x - x
  have hg_cont : ContinuousOn g (Set.Icc a b) := hf.sub continuousOn_id
  have hg0 : g a ≥ 0 := sub_nonneg_of_le (hmaps (Set.left_mem_Icc.mpr hab)).1
  have hg1 : g b ≤ 0 := sub_nonpos_of_le (hmaps (Set.right_mem_Icc.mpr hab)).2
  have hiv := intermediate_value_Icc' hab hg_cont
  exact Exists.elim (hiv ⟨hg1, hg0⟩) fun x hx => ⟨x, hx.1, sub_eq_zero.mp hx.2⟩

/-! ## Convergence on the grandfather paradox -/

/-- The grandfather action on the two-state phase space `alive/dead`: one
traversal flips the ancestor's status, so no state is fixed. -/
theorem grandfather_paradoxical : Paradoxical (Bool.not) := by
  intro x; cases x <;> decide

/-- **The grandfather loop is recurrent with period two.** Although paradoxical in
a single traversal, traversing the grandfather loop twice restores every state, so
the two-fold iterated grandfather loop is universally self-consistent. -/
theorem grandfather_recurrent : Bool.not^[2] = id := by
  decide

/-- Concretely, the two-fold grandfather loop is self-consistent (recurrence tames
the paradox without invoking a multiverse). -/
theorem grandfather_iterate_selfConsistent :
    SelfConsistent (iterate ⟨Bool.not⟩ 2) :=
  ⟨true, by decide⟩

/-! ## Examples and sanity checks -/

-- The identity loop is self-consistent (everyone is their own consistent history).
example : SelfConsistent (⟨id⟩ : CausalLoop Bool) := ⟨true, rfl⟩

-- The grandfather loop is *not* self-consistent in a single traversal.
example : ¬ SelfConsistent (⟨Bool.not⟩ : CausalLoop Bool) :=
  fun ⟨s, hs⟩ => grandfather_paradoxical s hs

#check @selfConsistent_conj
#check @loop_universally_consistent
#check @involution_fixedPoints_parity
#check @continuous_selfConsistent_Icc

end TimeTravelDeep

Hypothesis (Hypothesizer).  Five conjectures about causal loops beyond the
fixed-point existence layer:
  (H1) Self-consistency is invariant under bijective relabelling of world-states

  (H2) Self-consistency is compositional across a product of decoupled subsystems.
  (H3) [BOLD] On a finite phase space, every invertible loop is recurrent, and in

       state (a discrete Poincaré recurrence bridging fixed points and the finite
       group generated by the loop).
  (H4) [BOLD] For an involutive (time-reversal) loop on a finite phase space, the

  (H5) The analytic (Brouwer/IVT) guarantee holds on every compact phase

by an invertible loop on a finite set: its order N > 0 satisfies loopᴺ = id, so
loopᴺ fixes every state; per-state recurrence is the specialisation.  H4 follows
from the evenness of the support of an involution (its non-fixed points pair up),

symmetries/operations one can impose on a loop map — relabelling (H1), product

phenomenon; every invertible loop on a finite world is eventually self-consistent.

# AVD‑total chromatic number of central graphs of *regular* graphs

This file is a self‑contained companion to `Basic.lean`.  It specialises the theory
of **adjacent‑vertex‑distinguishing (AVD) total colourings** of the **central
graph** `C(G)` to the case where `G` is `d`‑regular, and proves the sharp

For a finite simple graph `H` we model a *total colouring* as a proper vertex
colouring of the **total graph** `T(H)` whose vertices are `V(H) ⊕ E(H)` and whose
edges join incident/adjacent objects.  A total colouring is **AVD** when adjacent
vertices receive distinct *colour sets*
`C(w) = {colour w} ∪ {colour e : e ∋ w}`.

The **central graph** `C(G)` is obtained from `G` by subdividing every edge once
and joining every pair of *non‑adjacent* vertices.  Its vertices are `V ⊕ E`; each
subdivision vertex has degree `2`, while **every original vertex has degree
`|V| − 1`**.
